title: Escaping the Verifier: Learning to Reason via Demonstrations
claim: A policy and critic sharing weights play an adversarial game, with critic verdicts mapped to rewards that drive RL updates for both.
layout: Single panel, left-to-right; crossing colored arrows from critic verdicts to two reward boxes
description: A single wide panel shows the method as a left-to-right flow. On the left, a red cylinder labeled Expert Data holds an open-book icon, and a blue Policy box below it holds a brain icon labeled Reasoning LLM. Both send arrows into a large central purple Relativistic Critic box, which shows a judge icon. A green dotted region marked Shared Weights encloses the critic and the policy. The critic lists three outputs: Choose Expert (red), Declare Tie (yellow), Choose Policy (blue). Color-coded arrows from these outputs cross over to a purple Reward for Critic box (1, τ_crit, 0) and a blue Reward for Policy box (0, τ_pol, 1). Dashed purple and blue arrows labeled RL update loop back to the critic and the policy. The crossing arrows draw the eye first.
caption: An overview of RARO. The method creates an adversarial game between a policy and a relativistic critic that share the same weights. The critic is rewarded for identifying the expert responses among (expert, policy) answer pairs, while the policy is rewarded for deceiving the critic. Additionally, the critic can declare a tie, yielding stable rewards when it is unsure. Both the policy and the critic are trained jointly via RL.
abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) to reason often relies on Reinforcement Learning (RL) with task-specific verifiers. However, many real-world reasoning-intensive tasks lack verifiers, despite offering abundant expert demonstrations that remain under-utilized for reasoning-focused training. We introduce RARO (Relativistic Adversarial Reasoning Optimization), which learns strong reasoning capabilities from expert demonstrations alone via Inverse Reinforcement Learning. RARO sets up an adversarial game between a policy and a relativistic critic: the policy learns to mimic expert answers, while the critic aims to identify the experts among expert-policy answer pairs. Both the policy and the critic are trained jointly and continuously via RL, and we identify the key stabilization techniques required for robust learning. Empirically, RARO significantly outperforms strong verifier-free baselines across all evaluation tasks: +13.7% accuracy on Countdown (1.5B), +8.2% accuracy on DeepMath (7B), and +19.1% win-rate on Poetry Writing (7B) against expert poems. RARO also exhibits similar robust scaling trends as RL with verifiers. These results demonstrate that RARO effectively elicits strong reasoning performance from expert demonstrations alone, enabling robust reasoning learning even when task-specific verifiers are unavailable.
